claims.text: Sustained plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy nanoscale multilayers is primarily controlled by interface-mediated dislocation nucleation and propagation.
Interface chemistry dictates local stress concentrations in these multilayers.
Layer thickness dictates local stress concentrations and short-range-order disruption.
The starting multilayer has relatively uniform short-range order.
Layer thickness and interfacial chemistry can be varied while retaining an FCC/BCC nanoscale multilayer structure.
Nanoindentation is suitable for small-scale creep characterization.
Local interface chemistry influences lattice distortion and short-range order.
Local stress concentrations at multilayer interfaces trigger dislocation nucleation under sustained load.
Segregating elemental additions at interfaces alter the energy barriers for dislocation emission and absorption.
Changes in dislocation emission and absorption barriers modulate the rate and spatial distribution of dislocation motion.
Interface-modulated dislocation motion produces progressive plastic deformation distinct from bulk dislocation slip.
Local disruption of short-range order near interfaces may facilitate or retard dislocation activity.
Thinner multilayer layers will produce slower creep rates than thicker layers.
Chemically enriched or tailored interfaces will produce slower creep rates and delay extensive plastic deformation relative to unmodified interfaces.
Modified interface chemistry will correlate with localized dislocation activity at interface regions.
Modified multilayers will exhibit altered spatial distributions of lattice distortion and short-range order.
Atomic diffusion and dislocation-mediated processes may make competing contributions to creep.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to nanoscale multilayers with intact interfaces and may fail after phase separation or loss of the multilayer structure.

A lack of systematic changes in creep rate, dislocation nucleation, and local short-range order after varying layer thickness and interface chemistry would falsify the proposed interface-governed mechanism.
